title: A Freeze Denial Overtaken by an Active Sev-2 Incident
scenario_text:
A release manager at Marigold Freight must decide whether a change can ship during the active change freeze, given how a comparable request was handled earlier in the same freeze.

**Decision A (2024-12-20)**
The routing team asked to deploy a change to the dispatch service during the freeze. DENIED. Note: 'The change was a routine latency optimization with no active incident behind it. Under the freeze policy, only changes remediating an active Sev-1 or Sev-2 incident may deploy, and none was open. Denied.'

**Current request C (2024-12-27)**
The same routing team asks to deploy essentially the same dispatch-service change. Since Decision A, NEW INFORMATION has emerged: at 06:14 today an active Sev-2 incident (INC-4471) was opened for elevated dispatch-assignment errors in production, and the on-call investigation identifies this exact change as the remediation. Monitoring shows customer-facing shipment delays.

**Change Freeze Policy (current, in force for this freeze)**
During the freeze, only changes that remediate an active Sev-1 or Sev-2 incident may deploy, and each such change must be signed off by a Director before it ships. All other changes — including routine optimizations — are blocked until the freeze lifts.

**Slack — #releases**
Eng: 'We already got told no on this dispatch change a week ago, so it's blocked — no point asking again.'
Release mgr: 'A week ago there was no incident. There's an active Sev-2 now and this change is the fix, so the situation isn't the same. Let me confirm the approval path.'

INC-4471 is confirmed active and tied to this change; the change is no longer a discretionary optimization.
question: Now that an active Sev-2 incident requires this change as its remediation, whose approval is required for it to deploy during the freeze?
